rv.q: Mr. Bartlett has given us what looks on first viewing like the best stage comedy to come along since Tom Stoppard's 'The Real Thing,' and Mr. Mayer's production is flat-out perfect.

As Bartlett tells it, with searing insight and mocking wit in a flawless production directed by Michael Mayer, this was the generation that grabbed everything with both hands — and then ate their young.

That includes Bartlett’s excoriating Love, Love Love, written six years ago and receiving its premiere here in a brilliantly cast production at the Roundabout Theatre Company’s off-Broadway Laura Pels Theatre.
It's a testament to Bartlett's clever, incisive dialogue that such selfish, limited people should steal our hearts.
Together the ensemble joins to create one of the most indelibly and viciously failed families to grace the contemporary stage.
Amy Ryan and Richard Armitage advance from the ages of 19 to 64 with a galloping satirical wit that pulls you along, happy and appalled, through the decades.
Director Michael Mayer’s faultless staging of the complex, time-shifting proceedings is further enhanced by Derek McLane’s multiple sets and Susan Hilfterty’s period-perfect costumes.

Mike Bartlett’s lacerating entertainment is less believably about a cultural and political generation than about the curdling of two outlandishly selfish individuals from larky young beauties to rich monster parents.

The outrageous and cliché behavior, meant to keep the tone comic even when it shouldn’t be, prevents the possibility of our taking seriously any intended argument about, say, the damage done to children, and society generally, when barriers to selfish behavior come down.
It all adds up to a well-paced production of a beautifully crafted, funny and poignant new play.

But even so, Love, Love, Love is a devilish delight, packed with the kind of uproarious surprises, ironic echoes, and self-consuming insights that are pretty rare in the theatre today, but that inspire joy in the most devoted whenever they appear.
"Love, Love, Love" left me both amused, and consumed by thoughts about fortune and fate.
Responses to Love, Love, Love are likely to vary based on what decade you were born, so if you were born between 1946 and 1964, take the kids!
Michael Mayer’s production also becomes increasingly more entertaining as the atmosphere becomes more combative and the performances hit ridiculous extremes.
Mike Bartlett's caustic comic takedown of British baby boomers is wildly funny and just as blunt.
Bartlett's writing–driven by the breathlessly hysterical tone of director Michael Mayer's production–is savagely and relentlessly funny in Kenneth and Sandra's scenes with their kids.
The play, nevertheless, can’t overcome its clichéd subject matter and is never quite as deeply meaningful as it intends to be.

Love, Love, Love might have redeemed itself if it contained a modicum of the love its title boasts, or if any of these characters had even the slightest bit of an arc, but — spoiler alert? — they don’t.
If you're going to indict an entire generation for its shallow values, your play is going to need more heft than this slick, superficial effort.
This play needs to be seen, produced and shown to a public that needs to laugh, needs to think and needs to be shown the truth.
Outstanding performances across the board, a smart trilogy of time-hopping sets and costumes, and a top-notch script make this bitter pill easy to swallow.
The comedy is superbly portrayed by this well-chosen cast—Armitage and Ryan the perfect yin and yang, ever so delicately brought to life by Michael Mayer's fine directorial hand.
Amy Ryan in particular raises her character to an art form as she energizes a larger-than-life persona in a performance that is as funny as it is award worthy.
Bartlett (Cock, King Charles III) is a great writer and a keen observer of relationships, and he proves as much with this decade-spanning serio-comedy...
These bitter questions about life come sugarcoated in a smart and fast-moving comedy, which makes them easy to swallow and take some time to digest after the show.
Under Mike Mayer's direction, five razor sharp cast members portray characters who are well-carved, poked at and picked apart for detailed authenticity.
The experience is more like binge watching three episodes of a BBC comedy, than viewing a cohesive piece of theater.
At the end of the day and play, The Beatles may repeatedly insist that love is all you need, but Bartlett wonders if it’s true.
But I had expected it to be more—and to be more subtle
I was enthralled by 'Love, Love, Love.' The cast was stellar.
This ensemble cast is superb... Sets, divine...Michael Mayer must have had so much fun directing this one.
It's kind of a bummer, even if there is truth in playwright Mike Bartlett's storytelling.

cn.t: Bartlett's scathing generational satire earns strong reviews for its biting wit and stellar performances from Ryan and Armitage, though some critics find its indictment of baby boomer selfishness too broad and one-dimensional.
